# Writing a VU0 kernel

VU0 is the PS2's *other* vector unit. Unlike VU1 it has no path to the screen —
it is a **coprocessor the CPU calls and reads back**. A kernel is: N quadwords
in, N quadwords out, one body run per element.

Put a `.cpp` under `src/vu0/`. Same setup as `src/vu/`: the framework is copied
in and the build compiles and runs your file to produce the microprogram plus an
EE-side driver.

```cpp
#include "vushader.hpp"

namespace {
struct Ranges : vu::Kernel {
  const char* name() const override { return "Ranges"; }
  int maxElements() const override { return 64; }

  void prepare(vu::Ctx& c) override { floor_ = vu::splat(c, 1e-6F); }
  vu::Vec floor_;

  void element(vu::Ctx& c) override {
    // c.position is one input quadword; write it and it is the output.
  }
};
}  // namespace
VU_KERNEL(Ranges);
```

The build writes a driver class named after the kernel, reachable through
`#include "scripts/vu0_kernels.gen.hpp"`:

```cpp
Tyra::RangesKernel k;
k.setParams(cam.x, cam.y, cam.z, 1.0F / 12.0F);
k.run(in, out, n);            // n <= maxElements()
```

## When a kernel is worth it

When the EE has **the same small piece of arithmetic to do for many things at
once**, over an array the game already has. The classic is "how far away is
everything?" — one subtract, one dot, one root per object — whose answers pick
levels of detail, decide what is worth drawing, set how loud a sound is and name
the thing the player is standing next to.

It is *not* worth it for one value, for anything branchy, or for work that would
be better done once and cached.

## The three constraints that shape every kernel

**1. `run()` BLOCKS the EE.** VU0's register file is the one COP2 macro mode
uses — the engine's own `Vec4`/`M4x4` math — so nothing may have vector
arithmetic in flight while the kernel runs. A few dozen elements is
microseconds; a big batch is not free, and the call is synchronous.

**2. There is no cross-element reduction.** No instruction adds a lane of
element 7 to a lane of element 8; the quadwords are independent by construction.
So a kernel computes the **terms** and the CPU folds them: find your minimum,
sum or count in an ordinary loop after `run()` returns. This is not a workaround,
it is the division of labour.

**3. It is small.** 256 quadwords of data memory total, and the default layout
leaves room for 112 elements each way; 512 instruction slots for the code. The
build refuses a layout that does not fit.

## Carrying an index through

`w` rides through untouched unless the body writes it, so put the array index
there and it comes back attached to the answer — no second array to keep in
step:

```cpp
in[i].set(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z, (float)i);
// ... after run():
int which = (int)out[i].w;
```

## Constants go in `prepare()`

A kernel's loop is a **real branch**, not three unrolled copies like the VU1
per-vertex body. A constant left in `element()` is therefore rebuilt for every
element — and the instruction that loads it is the one construct the host
simulator cannot model faithfully, because the assembler reorders it. Build
constants in `prepare()`; they are made once.

## The same rules as a VU1 program, where they apply

- **Never divide** (`divQ`, `rsqrtQ`) from the body — see the `tyra-vu-programs`
  skill; the reasoning is identical.
- Four scratch registers, `c.scratch(0..3)`.
- Guard the arithmetic yourself: something standing exactly on the camera makes
  `1/sqrt(0)` and spreads infinities through everything downstream, so floor the
  squared distance in `prepare()` and use it.

## Proving it is right, not just that it ran

"The kernel ran" and "the kernel is right" are different claims and only the
second is worth anything. Compute the same numbers on the EE once, at startup,
and compare:

```cpp
float d = sqrtf(dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz) - out[i].x;
```

`sqrtf` against VU0's reciprocal square root is a fair comparison — both are
single precision — so a disagreement is an arithmetic bug and not a tolerance
argument. This project's `Ranges` kernel agrees with the EE to about 1e-6 units.

## Where to look

- `src/vu0/*.cpp` in this project — the working examples.
- `vugen/vushader.hpp` — `vu::Kernel`, `vu::Ctx` and the free functions, all
  documented in the header. That is the reference.
- *Tools > VU Programs > VU0 kernel* also composes a kernel from a **stage list**
  with no C++ at all — worth checking before writing one, since the catalogue
  may already cover it.
